design_detail: Systematic review with random-effects meta-analysis (DerSimonian-Laird, Stata BE-17) for the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, by the RTI International-University of North Carolina Evidence-based Practice Center; PROSPERO CRD42022324376; an update of the 2014 AHRQ review and JAMA meta-analysis (Jonas et al.). Double-blind RCTs of at least 12 weeks of outpatient treatment in adults with alcohol use disorder, comparing nine medicines (acamprosate, disulfiram and naltrexone, approved by the FDA; baclofen, gabapentin, varenicline, topiramate, prazosin and ondansetron, off-label) with placebo or with each other; naltrexone analysed separately as oral 50 mg/day, oral 100 mg/day and long-acting injection. Searches November 2012 to September 2022 (earlier trials carried over from the 2014 review), surveillance and a PubMed update to 14 August 2023. 118 RCTs (156 articles), 20,976 participants; strength of evidence graded with AHRQ methods. A byline correction was published in 2024.
can_establish: The average difference between each medicine and placebo, in double-blind trials of 12 to 52 weeks mostly in middle-aged men with moderate to severe alcohol dependence who were abstinent at the start and received a psychosocial co-intervention, in the proportion returning to any drinking or to heavy drinking and in drinking days, with a graded strength of evidence, and the adverse effects reported in those trials.
cannot_establish: Effects in mild alcohol use disorder, in people still drinking at the start, in older or younger people, in trials shorter than 12 weeks or beyond 52 weeks; effects on mortality, injuries, crashes or quality of life (insufficient evidence for most medicines); which of naltrexone and acamprosate is better (head-to-head trials show no difference); rare or long-term harms; absolute effects in a given population (the numbers needed to treat are not reproducible); or whether the pooled estimates are affected by publication bias (not assessed).

sample.recruitment: PubMed, the Cochrane Library, CENTRAL, PsycINFO, CINAHL and EMBASE, English-language studies of adults, 1 November 2012 to 9 September 2022, run by a librarian and peer-reviewed by a second librarian with the PRESS checklist; reference lists of reviews and trials searched by hand; earlier trials taken from the 2014 review; article alerts after September 2022 and a PubMed update on 14 August 2023 found no new trials (Methods › Data Sources and Searches). Trial participants were recruited through treatment programmes, advertisements, referrals or a combination; US trials recruited largely by advertisement, while 15 of 22 trials in other countries recruited from inpatient settings (Results, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Applicability of Findings, 2nd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: adults with alcohol use disorder in outpatient treatment of at least 12 weeks with one of the nine medicines; double-blind RCTs against placebo or another listed medicine for efficacy; for harms also non-randomized, open-label, subgroup, cohort and case-control studies comparing two listed drugs (none were found). Outcomes: return to any drinking, return to heavy drinking (at least 4 drinks a day for women, 5 for men), percentage of drinking days and of heavy drinking days, drinks per drinking day, crashes, injuries, quality of life, function, mortality, adverse events (Methods › Study Selection). All participants met criteria for alcohol dependence in 103 of 118 trials; in 3 trials under 90% had alcohol use disorder (Results, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Limitations). Of 317 full texts, 267 were excluded: 80 for evidence type or design, 58 outcome, 50 intervention, 33 duplicate or superseded, 20 comparator, 13 population, 6 time period, 4 length of follow-up, 2 language, 1 setting (Figure 1).
sample.demographics: Mean age was typically 40 to 49 years, and only 21 trials enrolled younger or older populations; of 70 trials reporting race and sex, 63 enrolled mostly White men, and none recorded a sex other than male or female (Discussion › Applicability of Findings, 1st paragraph). Sample sizes 12 to 921 and treatment 12 to 52 weeks, as stated after the description of the 37 new trials. Of 23 acamprosate trials, 16 were in Europe and 4 in the US; of 49 naltrexone trials, 32 in the US and 8 in Europe (Results, 2nd paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level; attrition and handling of missing data were risk-of-bias criteria, but per-trial attrition is not given in the article.
sample.selection_effects: Mostly moderate to severe dependence, mostly White men aged 40 to 49, and most trials required a few days of abstinence before medication began (Discussion › Applicability of Findings). Most trials added a co-intervention (87 of 118 a psychosocial one; 100 of 118 any co-intervention such as medical management or counselling), so the estimates are of medication added to such treatment. English-language only; no grey-literature or trial-registry search is described, although one included result comes from a ClinicalTrials.gov record (ALK21-014, reference 16). Trials shorter than 12 weeks were excluded, as were four small disulfiram RCTs because of their designs and comparisons (Discussion, 3rd paragraph).

exposure.measurement: Randomized, double-blind assignment to a study medicine or placebo.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only: naltrexone analysed as oral 50 mg/day, oral 100 mg/day and long-acting injection, and pooled at any dose; the other medicines at the doses each trial gave, not analysed by dose; 12 to 52 weeks of treatment.
exposure.polysubstance: Not analysed. Other substance use followed each trial's criteria (per-trial characteristics are in eTable 4, not read). Some included trials enrolled people with co-occurring depression, bipolar disorder, PTSD, eating-disorder features or HIV (reference list).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; most trials required a few days of abstinence before medication started, and outcomes are drinking during treatment. Three trials in people not yet abstinent reported less heavy drinking with naltrexone or acamprosate than with placebo (Discussion › Applicability of Findings, 3rd paragraph).

comparison.controls: Placebo, in most trials with the same psychosocial co-intervention; or another listed medicine (four trials compared acamprosate with naltrexone directly).
comparison.matching: Randomization within trials. Two reviewers independently rated each trial's risk of bias as low, medium, high or unclear on randomization, allocation concealment, baseline similarity, masking, attrition, validity and reliability of measures, analysis and handling of missing data (Methods › Data Extraction, Risk-of-Bias Assessment, and Strength of Evidence); per-trial ratings are not shown in the article.

outcomes.instruments: Drinking outcomes as each trial reported them (methods of measurement not described in the article): return to any drinking and to heavy drinking as proportions; percentage of drinking days, percentage of heavy drinking days and drinks per drinking day as means; adverse events as reported, often without standardized measures or a described method of capture (Results › Adverse Effects, 1st paragraph).
outcomes.validity_norms: Heavy drinking is defined as at least 4 drinks a day for women and at least 5 for men; a drink is not defined in grams in the article.
outcomes.operationalization: The Methods name the primary outcome as alcohol consumption, defined in the analysis section as any alcohol use, return to heavy drinking and number of drinks per week; drinks per week is not reported, and drinks per drinking day is reported instead. Numbers needed to treat were calculated only for significant pooled RRs with at least moderate strength of evidence; the method is not described.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 35 counts the medicine-outcome cells of the Table with a numerical pooled or single-trial efficacy estimate across the five consumption outcomes; the text adds 2 head-to-head estimates and about 20 pooled adverse-effect estimates.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Only double-blind trials were eligible for efficacy, and masking was a risk-of-bias criterion. At review level, two reviewers independently screened, rated risk of bias and graded strength of evidence.

analysis.effect_sizes: Against placebo (Table): return to any drinking, acamprosate RR 0.88 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.93), 20 trials, 6380, NNT 11 (1 to 32), moderate; oral naltrexone 50 mg/day RR 0.93 (0.87 to 0.99), 16 trials, 2347, NNT 18 (4 to 32), moderate; 100 mg/day 0.97 (0.91 to 1.03), 3 trials, 946; injectable 0.96 (0.90 to 1.03), 2 trials, 939; any naltrexone 0.95 (0.92 to 0.99), 25 trials, 4604, moderate; baclofen 0.83 (0.70 to 0.98), 8 trials, 995, low; gabapentin 0.92 (0.83 to 1.02), 3 trials, 522, low; disulfiram 1.03 (0.90 to 1.17), 3 trials, 622, low (no effect). Return to heavy drinking: acamprosate 0.99 (0.94 to 1.05), 7 trials, 2496, moderate (no effect); naltrexone 50 mg/day 0.81 (0.72 to 0.90), 23 trials, 3170, NNT 11 (5 to 41), moderate; 100 mg/day 0.93 (0.84 to 1.01), 2 trials, 858; injectable 1.00 (0.82 to 1.21), 2 trials, 615; any naltrexone 0.86 (0.80 to 0.93), 27 trials, 4645, moderate; baclofen 0.92 (0.80 to 1.06), 4 trials, 483; gabapentin 0.90 (0.82 to 0.98), 3 trials, 522, low. Percentage of drinking days (WMD, percentage points): acamprosate -8.3 (-12.2 to -4.4), 14 trials, 4916, moderate; naltrexone 50 mg/day -5.1 (-7.16 to -3.04), 15 trials, 1992, moderate; any naltrexone -4.51 (-6.26 to -2.77), 24 trials, 4021, moderate; injectable -4.99 (-9.49 to -0.49 in the text; -9.49 to 0.49 in the Table), 2 trials, 467, low; topiramate -7.2 (-14.3 to -0.1), 8 trials, 1080, moderate. Percentage of heavy drinking days: naltrexone 50 mg/day -4.3 (-7.60 to -0.91), 7 trials, 624, moderate; injectable -4.68 (-8.63 to -0.73), 3 trials, 956, low; any naltrexone -3.92 (-5.86 to -1.97), 13 trials, 2167, moderate; topiramate -6.2 (-10.9 to -1.4), 9 trials, 1210, moderate. Drinks per drinking day: topiramate -2.0 (-3.1 to -1.0), 7 trials, 922, moderate; naltrexone 50 mg/day -0.49 (-0.92 to -0.06), 9 trials, 1018, low. Head-to-head, acamprosate against naltrexone: return to any drinking RR 1.03 (0.96 to 1.10), 3 trials, 800; return to heavy drinking 1.02 (0.93 to 1.11), 4 trials, 1141. Heterogeneity appears only in the figures: acamprosate, return to any drinking, I2 77.6% (tau-squared 0.01, Q(19) 84.97); naltrexone 50 mg/day, return to any drinking, I2 35.1%, return to heavy drinking I2 58.7%; acamprosate, return to heavy drinking, I2 0%. No prediction intervals. Editors' calculation, approximate, using the crude placebo event rates of Figures 2, 4 and 6: NNT about 10 (7 to 17) for acamprosate and about 21 (11 to 147) for naltrexone 50 mg/day for return to any drinking, and about 10 (7 to 19) for naltrexone 50 mg/day for return to heavy drinking.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable (aggregate data). Subgroup analyses by patient population (for example US against non-US trials) are mentioned without numerical results (Methods › Data Synthesis and Analysis).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42022324376; a full AHRQ technical report addressing five questions details methods and search strategies (Methods, 1st paragraph). The article reports no deviations; the PROSPERO record and technical report were not read, so the registration date and any deviations were not checked. Within the article, drinks per week is named as a primary measure but not reported, and restricted maximum likelihood sensitivity analyses are described but not reported.
analysis.selective_reporting: Results are presented only for medicines with at least low strength of evidence for benefit; ondansetron, varenicline and prazosin are relegated to eTable 5 (Results, 3rd paragraph). Sensitivity and subgroup results are not reported numerically; heterogeneity statistics appear only in the figures. Selective outcome reporting by trials is named as a limitation but was not assessed, and publication bias was not assessed.
analysis.power: Not addressed. Several cells rest on 1 to 3 trials (injectable and 100 mg/day naltrexone, gabapentin, disulfiram), where DerSimonian-Laird intervals tend to be too narrow.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Against placebo, about 12% fewer people on acamprosate and 7% fewer on oral naltrexone 50 mg/day returned to any drinking (relative reductions; moderate strength of evidence), and 19% fewer on naltrexone 50 mg/day returned to heavy drinking, with no effect of acamprosate on heavy drinking; both reduced drinking days. Topiramate reduced drinking days, heavy drinking days and drinks per drinking day (moderate) with more adverse effects. Acamprosate and naltrexone did not differ head to head. Evidence on mortality, injuries, crashes and quality of life was insufficient. Gastrointestinal adverse effects were more common with both acamprosate and naltrexone.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Key Points and abstract conclude that the findings "support oral naltrexone at 50 mg/d and acamprosate as first-line therapies" (Key Points › Meaning), with psychosocial interventions, and headline numbers needed to treat of 11 (95% CI 1 to 32) and 18 (4 to 32) to prevent one return to any drinking. Gaps: (1) the NNT intervals cannot come from the pooled RRs: a lower limit of 1 would mean every treated person benefits, whereas RR 0.88 (0.83 to 0.93) at the placebo event rate of Figure 2 corresponds to an NNT of about 10 (7 to 17), and RR 0.93 (0.87 to 0.99) for naltrexone to about 21 (11 to 147) (editors' calculation); (2) the abstract reports injectable naltrexone as 4.99 fewer drinking days over the 30-day period, while the analysed outcome is percentage of drinking days and the Table prints the interval as -9.49 to 0.49 (low strength of evidence); (3) the abstract does not say that acamprosate did not reduce return to heavy drinking (moderate strength of evidence for no effect) or that most US acamprosate trials found no benefit; (4) first-line status is the authors' clinical recommendation, resting on modest relative effects with moderate strength of evidence in trials of mostly White, middle-aged men with moderate to severe dependence who were abstinent at the start; the Discussion states these limits on applicability.

timeline.event: COMBINE trial (Anton et al., 2006), included here; it supplies the acamprosate and 100 mg/day naltrexone comparisons against placebo and one of the four head-to-head trials.
Jonas et al. AHRQ review and JAMA meta-analysis of outpatient pharmacotherapy for alcohol use disorders, which this review updates; 81 of its 118 RCTs come from it
Letter by Saitz on the 2014 review and reply by Jonas, Feltner and Garbutt (JAMA 2014;312:1349 and 1351), cited in this review's discussion of the limitations of small disulfiram trials.
This update: 37 new RCTs, searches to September 2022, surveillance to August 2023.
Correction notice, Error in Byline (JAMA 2024;332(16):1397; DOI 10.1001/jama.2024.11331): an author's middle initial corrected (Mark D. Edlund to Mark J. Edlund); no change to data or conclusions.

replication.where_it_stands: The most recent comprehensive synthesis for outpatient pharmacotherapy of alcohol use disorder, funded by AHRQ; its estimates update the 2014 review (jonas_2014) and share most of its trials, so the two are not independent evidence. The Cochrane reviews of acamprosate and of opioid antagonists on Tier A of the list (Rösner et al., 2010) cover many of the same trials and must not be counted as independent support. Read with its reporting problems (non-reproducible NNT intervals, unlabelled heterogeneity P values, and an acamprosate heavy-drinking forest plot that includes head-to-head comparisons); the editors' recalculation without those comparisons leaves the null acamprosate heavy-drinking result unchanged.

funding.funder: Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ), US Department of Health and Human Services, contract 75Q80120D00007, task order 75Q80122F32004. AHRQ nominated and selected the topic; an AHRQ representative served as contracting officer's representative, provided technical assistance and commented on drafts of the full evidence report, but AHRQ did not take part in the literature search, eligibility criteria, data analysis or interpretation, or the preparation, review or approval of the manuscript (Article notes › Funding/Support; Role of the Funder/Sponsor).
funding.declared_conflicts: None reported (Article notes › Conflict of Interest Disclosures).
funding.affiliations_note: RTI International-University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Evidence-based Practice Center, RTI International, Kaiser Permanente Center for Health Research (Portland, Oregon) and The Ohio State University. The senior author (Jonas) led the 2014 review that this one updates. Acknowledged contributors, none compensated, include staff of AHRQ, the American Psychiatric Association and the American Society of Addiction Medicine (Additional Contributions).

what_would_settle_it: Placebo-controlled and head-to-head trials in the groups the evidence lacks (women, older and younger adults, mild alcohol use disorder, people still drinking at the start), with standardized adverse-event capture and follow-up of health outcomes (injuries, hospital admission, mortality) beyond a year; and an individual-participant meta-analysis of the existing trials, with registry searches for unpublished trials, to test publication bias and estimate absolute effects by baseline risk.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Adults with alcohol use disorder, nine named medicines, placebo or another listed medicine, consumption, health and harm outcomes, outpatient setting and minimum duration are specified.
A PROSPERO registration and a full technical report with methods are cited; the article does not say the protocol preceded the review or report deviations (the registry record was not read).

Double-blind RCTs of at least 12 weeks for efficacy, because shorter trials may mislead given fluctuating drinking; observational and non-randomized designs added for harms because trials are too small and short for rare harms.

Six databases, librarian-run and PRESS-reviewed strategies (in the technical report), reference lists, surveillance to August 2023 and a recent search; but English-language only without a stated reason (2 full texts excluded for language), and no grey literature or trial registries described. AMSTAR 2 gives partial yes only if such restrictions are justified (decision p-amstar2-item4).
Two investigators independently reviewed each title and abstract and each full text, with a third senior reviewer for disagreements.
Structured forms, with at least two investigators reviewing every extraction for completeness and accuracy, which meets the item's consensus criterion.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Figure 1 gives the number excluded for each of ten reasons, but neither the article nor, by its list of contents, the supplement lists the excluded studies; the AHRQ technical report may, and was not read.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Provisional: per-study characteristics are in eTable 4 of the supplement (not read), and only for the 37 new trials; the article gives aggregate descriptions and, in Figures 2 to 6, each trial's duration and arm sizes.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Two independent reviewers rated randomization, concealment, baseline similarity, masking, attrition, measures, analysis and missing data; selective reporting is not among the listed criteria (the limitations say it may have occurred), and per-trial ratings are not shown in the article.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported
domains.note: Provisional: not reported in the article; whether eTable 4 records trial funding is unknown (supplement not read).

Random-effects RRs and WMDs are suitable in themselves, but Figure 5 (acamprosate against placebo, return to heavy drinking) includes rows whose comparator counts are those of the naltrexone arms in Figure 6 (Morley 2006, 39 of 53; Mann 2013, 86 of 169; Anton 2006, 207 of 309), so head-to-head contrasts are pooled as placebo comparisons and shared acamprosate arms are counted twice; Figure 3 (disulfiram) also enters shared arms twice; DerSimonian-Laird intervals from 2 or 3 trials are reported without the described sensitivity results.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Risk of bias enters the strength-of-evidence grades, but no analysis of its effect on the pooled estimates is reported.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: Every conclusion carries a strength-of-evidence grade built from risk of bias, consistency, directness and precision, and the Discussion uses those grades.

I2 is computed (shown in the figures) and subgroups by population (US against non-US) were analysed; the Discussion explains the absence of benefit of acamprosate in US trials by recruitment and health-system differences. A close call: the subgroup results are not given and the I2 of 77.6% for acamprosate is not discussed in the text.
Not investigated or discussed; only selective outcome reporting by trials is named as a limitation.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding, the funder's role and the authors' disclosures (none) are reported.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Provisional: items 8 and 10 can be judged only from Supplement 1, which was not read; neither is a critical item, so they cannot change the overall rating. Four critical items are 'no' (4: English-only search without justification; 7: no list of excluded studies; 11: a headline pool mixes head-to-head and placebo comparisons and counts shared arms twice; 15: publication bias not assessed), which under AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence; items 2 and 9 are partly met and 13 is met. This rates the review as an unbiased summary, not the trials, whose own risk of bias the review graded but does not show per trial. The practical consequences are limited for the main estimates: the editors' recalculation of Figure 5 without the active-comparator rows gives RR 0.99 (0.95 to 1.05), and the disulfiram estimate is null whichever control groups are used. The review may be cited for the pooled RRs and WMDs of acamprosate and oral naltrexone 50 mg/day against placebo with the review's strength-of-evidence grades, for the head-to-head null, for the topiramate drinking-day results and for the adverse-effect RRs; it should not be cited for its NNT intervals, for absolute effects, for injectable or 100 mg/day naltrexone as established (2 or 3 trials, low strength of evidence), or for health outcomes.

key_findings.finding: 2860 citations were screened, 317 full texts reviewed and 267 excluded; 50 new articles (37 RCTs) and 106 articles (81 RCTs) from the 2014 review gave 156 articles reporting 118 RCTs with 20,976 participants: 111 trials contributed consumption outcomes, 31 health outcomes and 99 adverse events. No observational study of harms was found, so all harms data come from RCTs.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1 (flow chart, image); Key Points

key_findings.finding: All participants met criteria for alcohol dependence in 103 of 118 trials; 87 (73.7%) of 118 trials included a psychosocial co-intervention, and 100 of 118 a co-intervention such as medical management, harm reduction or counselling; of 23 acamprosate trials 16 were in Europe and 4 in the US, and of 49 naltrexone trials 32 were in the US and 8 in Europe. Mean age was typically 40 to 49 years, and 63 of the 70 trials reporting race and sex enrolled mostly White men.
key_findings.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Applicability of Findings, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Acamprosate against placebo: return to any drinking RR 0.88 (95% CI 0.83 to 0.93), 20 trials, 6380 participants, moderate strength of evidence, NNT 11 (1 to 32); return to heavy drinking RR 0.99 (0.94 to 1.05), 7 trials, 2496, moderate strength of evidence for no effect; percentage of drinking days WMD -8.3 (-12.2 to -4.4), 14 trials, 4916, moderate; heavy drinking days and drinks per drinking day insufficient.
key_findings.locator: Table (Acamprosate column); Results › Alcohol Consumption Outcomes, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Figure 2 shows I2 77.6% (tau-squared 0.01, Q(19) 84.97, P < .001) for return to any drinking, not reported in the text; its 20 trials sum to 5931 participants (editors' arithmetic), not 6380. The two trials with RRs above 1 are Mason 2006 (1.04, 1.00 to 1.09) and Berger 2013 (1.15, 0.99 to 1.34), the latter in US family medicine.

key_findings.finding: Oral naltrexone 50 mg/day against placebo: return to any drinking RR 0.93 (0.87 to 0.99), 16 trials, 2347, moderate, NNT 18 (4 to 32); return to heavy drinking RR 0.81 (0.72 to 0.90), 23 trials, 3170, moderate, NNT 11 (5 to 41); percentage of drinking days WMD -5.1 (-7.16 to -3.04), 15 trials, 1992, moderate; percentage of heavy drinking days WMD -4.3 (-7.60 to -0.91), 7 trials, 624, moderate; drinks per drinking day WMD -0.49 (-0.92 to -0.06), 9 trials, 1018, low. At any dose: return to any drinking 0.95 (0.92 to 0.99), 25 trials, 4604; return to heavy drinking 0.86 (0.80 to 0.93), 27 trials, 4645; both moderate.
key_findings.locator: Table (Naltrexone columns); Results › Alcohol Consumption Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Figures 4 and 6 (images)
key_findings.note: Figure 4 shows 20 comparisons with 2719 participants at 50 mg/day for return to any drinking (I2 35.1%), against 16 trials and 2347 in the Table; the text gives the heavy-drinking NNT as based on 19 trials and 2875 participants, against 23 trials and 3170 in the Table and Figure 6 (I2 58.7%).

key_findings.finding: Other naltrexone forms against placebo: oral 100 mg/day, return to any drinking RR 0.97 (0.91 to 1.03), 3 trials, 946, and return to heavy drinking 0.93 (0.84 to 1.01), 2 trials, 858, low (no effect); injectable, return to any drinking 0.96 (0.90 to 1.03), 2 trials, 939, and return to heavy drinking 1.00 (0.82 to 1.21), 2 trials, 615, low (no effect); injectable, percentage of drinking days WMD -4.99 (-9.49 to -0.49), 2 trials, 467, and heavy drinking days WMD -4.7 (-8.6 to -0.73), 3 trials, 956, low.
key_findings.locator: Table (Naltrexone 100 mg/d and Injection columns); Results › Alcohol Consumption Outcomes, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: The Table prints the injectable drinking-days interval as -9.49 to 0.49, which would not exclude no difference; the text's -0.49 is the value centred on the estimate (editors' arithmetic). The abstract reports this result in days rather than percentage points.

key_findings.finding: Disulfiram against placebo did not prevent return to any drinking: RR 1.03 (0.90 to 1.17), 3 trials, 622, low strength of evidence for no effect (range 22.7% to 81.2% with disulfiram, 34.4% to 88.1% with placebo); percentage of drinking days, 2 trials, 290, no significant difference, insufficient. Four small disulfiram RCTs (15 or fewer treated people each) were ineligible because of their designs and comparisons.
key_findings.locator: Table (Disulfiram column); Results › Alcohol Consumption Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Figure 3 pools five comparisons, entering each Fuller trial's disulfiram arm against two control groups, and gives 0.99 (0.92 to 1.06). The Table's 1.03 (0.90 to 1.17), n = 622, is reproduced by using the second control group of each Fuller trial with Petrakis 2005; the first control groups give 0.94 (0.86 to 1.03) (editors' recalculation, DerSimonian-Laird). Null either way.

key_findings.finding: Off-label medicines against placebo: topiramate reduced percentage of drinking days (WMD -7.2, -14.3 to -0.1; 8 trials, 1080), percentage of heavy drinking days (-6.2, -10.9 to -1.4; 9 trials, 1210) and drinks per drinking day (-2.0, -3.1 to -1.0; 7 trials, 922), all moderate strength of evidence; topiramate and crashes or injuries, 2 trials, 541, reduced risk, low. Baclofen: return to any drinking RR 0.83 (0.70 to 0.98), 8 trials, 995, low (imprecision and inconsistency), no effect on other outcomes. Gabapentin: return to any drinking 0.92 (0.83 to 1.02) and return to heavy drinking 0.90 (0.82 to 0.98), 3 trials, 522, low. Ondansetron, varenicline and prazosin had low or insufficient evidence and are not reported.
key_findings.locator: Table (Baclofen, Gabapentin and Topiramate columns); Results › Alcohol Consumption Outcomes, 2nd paragraph; Results, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Head to head, acamprosate and naltrexone did not differ: return to any drinking RR 1.03 (0.96 to 1.10), 3 trials, 800; return to heavy drinking RR 1.02 (0.93 to 1.11), 4 trials, 1141 (references 19, 37, 45 and 48: COMBINE, Kiefer 2003, Mann 2013, Morley 2006).
key_findings.locator: Results › Alcohol Consumption Outcomes, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Health outcomes were infrequently reported and the evidence was insufficient for most medicines: deaths, acamprosate 7 against 6 with placebo (8 trials, 2677), baclofen 8 against 3 (4 trials, 660), naltrexone 1 against 2 (6 trials, 1738); quality of life or function no significant difference or conflicting results; crashes or injuries reduced only with topiramate (low).
key_findings.locator: Table (Motor vehicle crashes or injuries; Quality of life or function; Mortality rows); Results › Health Outcomes, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Adverse effects against placebo (RR, 95% CI): naltrexone, dizziness 1.99 (1.47 to 2.69), nausea 1.73 (1.51 to 1.98), vomiting 1.53 (1.23 to 1.91); acamprosate, diarrhoea 1.58 (1.27 to 1.97); baclofen, dizziness 1.89 (1.40 to 2.55), drowsiness 1.46 (1.15 to 1.86), numbness 7.78 (1.42 to 42.56), sleepiness 1.81 (1.11 to 2.97); topiramate, dizziness 2.29 (1.39 to 3.78), paraesthesia 3.08 (2.11 to 4.49), taste abnormalities 3.01 (1.70 to 5.34), cognitive dysfunction 2.37 (1.58 to 3.55); gabapentin, cognitive dysfunction 2.76 (1.51 to 5.06), dizziness 1.70 (1.24 to 2.32). Head to head, nausea RR 0.56 (0.35 to 0.88) and vomiting 0.60 (0.39 to 0.93) with acamprosate against naltrexone. Figure 7 grades withdrawal from trials because of adverse events with naltrexone as moderate strength of evidence for harm. Adverse events were often not collected with standardized measures.
key_findings.locator: Results › Adverse Effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 7 (image)

key_findings.finding: Of the US acamprosate trials, most found no significant benefit on return to any or heavy drinking; US trials recruited largely by advertisement, while 15 of 22 trials elsewhere recruited from inpatient settings where withdrawal may have been managed and medication started before discharge, which the authors offer as the explanation. Applicability to mild alcohol use disorder, to people aged 65 or over or in their 20s, and to people not yet abstinent is uncertain.
key_findings.locator: Discussion › Applicability of Findings, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
key_findings.note: This passage counts 5 US acamprosate trials; the Results count 4.

key_findings.finding: Methods: random-effects meta-analysis with the DerSimonian-Laird estimator and restricted maximum likelihood sensitivity analyses when pooled effects were significant (results not reported); RRs and WMDs with 95% CIs; I2 for heterogeneity; subgroups by patient population; NNTs only for significant RRs with at least moderate strength of evidence; strength of evidence graded high, moderate, low or insufficient by two reviewers. English-language studies only; PROSPERO CRD42022324376.
key_findings.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph; Methods › Data Sources and Searches; Methods › Data Extraction, Risk-of-Bias Assessment, and Strength of Evidence, 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Methods › Data Synthesis and Analysis

reporting_issues.issue: The NNT intervals (acamprosate 11, 1 to 32; naltrexone 50 mg/day 18, 4 to 32, for return to any drinking; 11, 5 to 41, for return to heavy drinking) cannot be derived from the pooled RRs, and the method is not described. A lower limit of 1 would mean that every treated person benefits. Using the crude placebo event rates of Figures 2, 4 and 6, the pooled RRs give NNTs of about 10 (7 to 17), 21 (11 to 147) and 10 (7 to 19) (editors' calculation, approximate).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Key Points; Abstract › Results; Results › Alcohol Consumption Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table; Figures 2, 4 and 6
reporting_issues.consequence: The NNT intervals, which headline the abstract, should not be cited; if an NNT is given it should be recomputed from the RR and a stated baseline risk, and the naltrexone NNT for return to any drinking is far less precise than printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The P values printed beside the pooled estimates in the Results are, where they can be checked, the heterogeneity (Q test) P values shown in the figures, not tests of the pooled effect, and they are not labelled. For example injectable naltrexone, return to any drinking, RR 0.96 (0.90 to 1.03), P = .14, matches Q(1) = 2.20, P = .14 in Figure 4; topiramate drinks per drinking day WMD -2.0 (-3.1 to -1.0) is printed with P = .19, although its interval implies P < .001, and baclofen RR 0.83 (0.70 to 0.98) with P < .001, although its interval implies P of about .03 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Alcohol Consumption Outcomes, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results › Adverse Effects, 2nd paragraph; Figures 2 to 6
reporting_issues.consequence: Read as effect tests, these P values contradict the intervals; claims must use the CIs and must not quote these P values as significance tests.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 5 (acamprosate against placebo, return to heavy drinking) has 11 rows from 7 trials; in four trials the acamprosate arm appears twice, and in three the second comparator matches the naltrexone arm of the same trial in Figure 6 (Morley 2006, 39 of 53, where the placebo arm has 61; Mann 2013, 86 of 169, where the placebo arm has 85; Anton 2006, 207 of 309). The figure's pooled RR is 1.00 (0.96 to 1.04); the Table and text give 0.99 (0.94 to 1.05). The editors' recalculation (DerSimonian-Laird) reproduces the figure from its 11 rows and gives 0.99 (0.95 to 1.05) from the 7 placebo-controlled rows.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Figures 5 and 6 (images); Table; Results › Alcohol Consumption Outcomes, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The plotted pool mixes head-to-head acamprosate-naltrexone contrasts into a placebo comparison and double counts participants; the four repeated rows sum to 1141 participants, the head-to-head n, of which COMBINE supplies 612 (second reader's count from Figure 5; the same split follows from Jonas et al., 2014, Figure 3); the conclusion of no effect on return to heavy drinking survives their removal, but the figure should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Counts of trials and participants differ between the Table, the text and the figures: acamprosate, return to any drinking, 6380 participants in the Table against 5931 summed from the 20 trials of Figure 2; naltrexone 50 mg/day, return to any drinking, 16 trials and 2347 participants in the Table and text against 20 comparisons and 2719 participants in Figure 4; naltrexone 50 mg/day, return to heavy drinking, NNT said to rest on 19 trials and 2875 participants against 23 trials and 3170 in the Table and Figure 6 (editors' arithmetic from the figures).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table; Results › Alcohol Consumption Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Figures 2, 4 and 6
reporting_issues.consequence: Trial and participant numbers in claims should be stated as the Table's, with the caveat that the figures do not reproduce them.

reporting_issues.issue: The injectable naltrexone percentage-of-drinking-days result is given as WMD -4.99 (-9.49 to -0.49) in the text and (-9.49 to 0.49) in the Table, and the abstract reports it as 4.99 fewer drinking days over the 30-day treatment period, although the outcome is percentage of drinking days. The acamprosate heavy-drinking-days estimate, WMD -3.4 (-6.45 to 5.86), is not centred in its interval (midpoint -0.30; editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Results; Results › Alcohol Consumption Outcomes, 1st paragraph; Table
reporting_issues.consequence: The injectable result should be cited, if at all, as a difference in percentage points from 2 trials with low strength of evidence; the acamprosate heavy-drinking-days figure is unreliable as printed (insufficient evidence in any case).

reporting_issues.issue: Internal counts disagree: co-interventions in 87 (73.7%) of 118 trials and, two sentences later, in 100 of 118 (perhaps psychosocial against any co-intervention, which the article does not say); 4 US acamprosate trials in the Results and 5 in the Discussion; the acamprosate range for return to heavy drinking is printed as 41.9% to 81.5%, while the highest acamprosate rate in Figure 5 is 85.1% (Chick 2000); gabapentin dizziness is given twice with the same RR (1.70, 1.24 to 2.32; P = .83) but different event-rate ranges (6.5% to 7.8% against 3.8% to 6.0%; and 21.2% to 56.8% against 13.7% to 32.6%).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results, 2nd paragraph; Results › Adverse Effects, 2nd paragraph; Discussion › Applicability of Findings, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the share of trials with co-interventions and the gabapentin dizziness rates should not be quoted from this article without checking the supplement.

reporting_issues.issue: Citation numbers in the figures do not always match the reference list: Figure 2 cites reference 26 (a naltrexone trial by its title) for Chick 2000, whose acamprosate trial (UKMAS) is reference 27, while Figures 4 and 6 cite 27 for Chick's naltrexone trial; Figure 2 labels the COMBINE acamprosate comparison 'Anton et al, 17 2005' (reference 17 is a naltrexone trial), although it shares its placebo arm (254 of 309) with Anton 2006 (reference 19) in Figure 4.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Figures 2, 4 and 6 (images); References 17, 19, 26 and 27
reporting_issues.consequence: Trials cannot be identified from the figure citations alone; anchors to individual trials must use the trial data, not the reference numbers.

reporting_issues.issue: Table footnotes appear misplaced: footnote k, about one accidental death and injuries in acamprosate trials and a traffic accident on acamprosate, is attached to the naltrexone quality-of-life cell, while footnote e, attached to the acamprosate crashes-or-injuries cell (0 studies), repeats the wording of footnote j.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table, footnotes e, j and k
reporting_issues.consequence: The acamprosate injury information is attached to the wrong cell; the Table's zero count for acamprosate crashes or injuries conflicts with the injuries the footnote describes.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods define the primary outcome as including number of drinks per week, which is not reported; drinks per drinking day is reported instead. The text also says characteristics of trials new since 2104 (for 2014), and the Methods judge significance by whether intervals cross 0, which does not apply to risk ratios.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Data Synthesis and Analysis; Results, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the drinks-per-week outcome is unreported.

reporting_issues.issue: The Results text says that gabapentin was not significantly associated with lower return to any drinking (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.02) or with a significant reduction in return to heavy drinking (RR 0.90, 0.82 to 0.98), although the second interval excludes 1; the Table and the Discussion treat the heavy-drinking result as low-strength evidence of benefit. The P value printed beside it (.75) is probably a heterogeneity test (reporting issue 1).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Results › Alcohol Consumption Outcomes, 2nd paragraph; Table)
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims citing the gabapentin heavy-drinking result should use the Table's estimate and grade and note that the text calls it not significant.
